title: Query Optimisation: Costing
lead: Before choosing a join, predict how many rows will reach it. Derive those predictions from visible counts and inspect the assumptions that can make them wrong.
goals: Estimate operator costs and the cardinalities passed between steps
Read catalog statistics and explain when they need updating
Calculate selectivity for equality, range, NOT, AND, and OR conditions

sections.title: Predict the rows each later operator must process
sections.html:
A join choice depends on how many outer rows will probe the inner side. Before running the query, those rows do not exist yet. The optimizer therefore needs an estimate of each intermediate result. The number of rows is its cardinality. An estimate leaving one operator becomes an input estimate for the next.

Use an original Employees fixture: 12,000 rows on 240 pages, 40 distinct departments, and a second condition expected to retain 20% of rows. We want one department plus that second condition. If departments have equal frequencies, one department contributes 12,000/40=300 rows. If the second condition has the same 20% frequency within that department, 300×0.2=60 survive.

Those are two distinct assumptions. Uniformity spreads rows equally over department values. Independence says knowing the department does not change the second condition's probability. Neither follows merely from having 40 department names.

StepRows enteringEstimated rows leavingWork
Heap scan12,000 stored12,000240 page reads
Department filter12,00030012,000 checks
Second filter30060300 checks
Projection606060 row-processing steps

We scan the heap once, not once for each operator. Suppose one page read costs one abstract unit and each listed CPU step costs 0.001 units. Cost is 240+0.001×(12,000+300+60)=252.36 units. This illustrates the System R combination of I/O and weighted tuple processing. It is not a measured time, and 60 output rows are not 60 page reads.

The catalog stores approximate statistics: row and page counts, distinct-value counts, min/max values, and index height. It may store histograms too. Collecting exact fresh statistics after every change would itself cost work; systems refresh periodically or on request, such as ANALYZE. If the data grows or becomes skewed, stale statistics can understate the rows reaching a join and therefore understate its probes or memory needs.

The selectivity of a filter is its surviving fraction: 300/12,000=0.025 for the first filter. “Highly selective” conventionally means it keeps very few rows, so the numeric fraction is small. Write “fraction retained” beside the number to avoid reversing it.

Key takeaway

Selectivity is the fraction retained, not the fraction discarded. “Highly selective” usually describes a condition that retains very few rows, meaning its selectivity value is small.

sections.title: Derive a formula by counting the rows it represents
sections.html:
Start with equality. If A has V(A)=40 actual distinct values, each equally frequent, choosing one existing value keeps one of 40 equal shares. Thus sel(A=c)=1/V(A). If c is known to be absent, the estimate should be zero; the equal-share argument assumes c belongs to the domain.

For a discrete range, list eligible values before using a formula. Integers 10 through 29 give 20 values. A>24 keeps 25,26,27,28,29: five values, so selectivity 5/20=0.25. A continuous uniform interval [10,30] instead measures length: above 24 occupies 6/20=0.30. A single endpoint has nonzero mass in the integer model and zero mass in the continuous one. Clip estimates to [0,1]; a one-value domain must be tested directly rather than dividing by a zero interval width.

Combine conditions on a 100-row population with no NULLs. P keeps 20, Q keeps 30. If independent, their overlap is 0.2×0.3×100=6 rows.

ConditionCount reasoningSelectivity
NOT P100−20=801−0.2=0.8
P AND Q6 in both0.2×0.3=0.06
P OR Q20+30−6=440.2+0.3−0.06=0.44

We subtract the overlap for OR because those six rows were counted twice. Independence supplies the overlap; without it, use evidence about the actual overlap. SQL NULL adds UNKNOWN, which WHERE discards. Then NOT P need not retain every row P discarded, so the complement formula needs a NULL-aware model.

Why an equality join can produce more rows than either table

Let R contain 600 rows over 30 keys and S contain 900 over 60 keys. Assume uniform frequencies and that R's key set is contained in S's. For each common key, R has 600/30=20 rows and S has 900/60=15. That key produces 20×15=300 pairs. Thirty common keys give 9,000 rows, equivalently 600×900/max(30,60).

The max-distinct-values formula therefore rests on uniformity and key-set containment. With a valid non-NULL foreign key from S to unique R, we have stronger information: every S row matches exactly one R row, so the result is exactly |S|. Nullable foreign-key rows with NULL do not match in this equijoin.

Why not estimate the general join as min(600,900)?

Neither side's join key is unique. Every same-key row can pair with multiple rows on the other side. The 20-by-15 calculation exposes those multiplicities.

Key takeaway

The multiplication formula requires independence. If the conditions are correlated, their overlap is not s1s2. SQL NULL introduces UNKNOWN, so even the formula for NOT needs to be reconsidered.

sections.title: Use local buckets when one global average hides skew
sections.html:
The equal-frequency model treats rare and frequent values alike. Suppose most employees are concentrated in a few ages. Keeping every exact frequency is expensive, but keeping one global average is too crude. A histogram divides the domain into adjacent buckets and stores counts for each.

Start with an original equi-width histogram over integers: [1,4] contains 20 rows and [5,8] contains 60. The intervals are equally wide, but the counts differ. To estimate A=6, locate [5,8] and divide its 60 rows across four values: 15. For A>6, only 7 and 8 remain in that bucket, so 2/4×60=30 rows. For A>3, take one quarter of the first bucket plus all of the second: 5+60=65.

This still assumes uniformity inside each bucket. It does not claim each real value in [5,8] has exactly 15 occurrences. More buckets improve resolution but occupy more catalog space.

An equi-depth histogram instead aims for equal row counts and allows interval widths to differ. Consider [1,3], [4,9], [10,12], with 30 rows each.

BucketInteger valuesRowsEstimated rows per value
[1,3]33010
[4,9]6305
[10,12]33010

A=5 estimates five rows; A=11 estimates ten. Equal depth does not imply equal width. For A≥7, the second bucket contributes 7,8,9: 3/6×30=15. The third contributes all 30, total 45 of 90 rows, selectivity 0.5.

For 2≤A≤10, calculate each contribution separately: [1,3] supplies 2 and 3, so 2/3×30=20; [4,9] supplies all 30; [10,12] supplies only 10, so 1/3×30=10. Total 60, selectivity 2/3. Counting inclusive integer endpoints prevents a common off-by-one error.

When statistics are missing, systems fall back to default selectivities. The lecture illustrates historical PostgreSQL 13 constants; a default is a policy assumption, not a measured frequency or a version-independent truth. Better single-column buckets still do not establish independence between different columns.

Which uncertainty remains even if the bucket totals are exact?

The frequencies inside a partially selected bucket may be uneven. Its estimated fraction can differ from its actual qualifying count. Correlation with another column remains a separate uncertainty.

sections.title: Exercise: expose a bad independence estimate
sections.html:
There are 10,000 people. Twenty percent live in city X; twenty percent have a postcode in region X. In this fixture the two predicates match exactly the same people. Estimate their AND using independence, then compute the actual count. Explain how a correct single-column histogram can still leave the error.

Compare assumption with data

Independence predicts 10,000×0.2×0.2=400 rows. Actual overlap is the whole 20% group, so 2,000 rows qualify. The actual count is five times the estimate. Each individual 20% estimate was correct; the error came from multiplying as though the groups were independent.

For OR, independence would predict 0.2+0.2−0.04=0.36, or 3,600 rows. Actual OR is again the same group, 2,000. Seeing both calculations makes the overlap assumption visible.

Now imagine these rows form an indexed-nested-loop outer input with one uncached data read per probe. Ignoring the common acquisition cost, the estimated probe work is 400 reads but actual work is 2,000. Another join estimated at 900 units might have been preferable. This supplied comparison explains why cardinality errors matter; it is not a benchmark or a claim that every optimizer makes this exact choice.

When diagnosing a plan, locate the earliest large estimated-versus-actual row mismatch. Check freshness, skew, NULL assumptions, and correlation before changing the algorithm above it. One false input estimate can make several later estimates look wrong.

quiz.question: An equi-width bucket contains 4 values and 60 rows. What is the estimated equality count for one value?
quiz.explanation: Assuming uniformity within the bucket gives 60/4=15. This is an estimate based on equal frequencies, not the actual count if the data is skewed.
